```{r}
#| echo: FALSE

devtools::load_all()
library(knitr)
```

This is a temporary document for the illustration and discussion of the new "results of a call to
`nextBest()`" class. It can be deleted once the development is complete.

## Test data

```{r}

# This is a slight variation of the nextBest example file.  The differences being a coarser
# dose grid so that the output is shorter, and a larger sample count so that probabilties of
# overdose are more meaningful.

# Create the data.
my_data <- Data(
  x = c(0.1, 0.5, 1.5, 3, 6, 10, 10, 10),
  y = c(0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 0),
  ID = 1:8,
  cohort = c(0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 5, 5),
  doseGrid = c(0.1, 0.5, 1.5, 3, 6, seq(from = 10, to = 80, by = 10))
)

# Initialize the CRM model used to model the data.
my_model <- LogisticLogNormal(
  mean = c(-0.85, 1),
  cov = matrix(c(1, -0.5, -0.5, 1), nrow = 2),
  ref_dose = 56
)

# Set-up some MCMC parameters and generate samples from the posterior.
my_options <- McmcOptions(burnin = 5, step = 1, samples = 1000)
my_samples <- mcmc(my_data, my_model, my_options)

# Define the rule for dose increments and calculate the maximum dose allowed.
my_increments <- IncrementsRelative(
  intervals = c(0, 20),
  increments = c(1, 0.33)
)
next_max_dose <- maxDose(my_increments, data = my_data)
```

## Progress to date

At the moment, the `recommend` methods are essentially simple copies of the existing `nextBest`
methods, with all references to graphing (in both the arguments and body) removed. They return an
object of class `Recommendion` (or a subclass) rather than a `list`. The only subclass I've
implemented so far is `RecommendationProbs`, which adds an arbitrary array of probabilities.

The `recommend` and `tidy` methods are in `Rules-methods1.R`, to minimise the chance of conflicts
with other changes. (The `plot` methods, when written, will join them.) Once the code is more
stable, it can be moved to `Rules-methods.R` and the new file deleted. The `knit_print` methods are
in `helpers_knitr_Recommendation.R`.

Tests exist for all `recommend` methods. As before, they are essentially copies of the existing
tests for `nextBest` calls. References to plots have been removed and they test that the
recommendation returned by `nextBest` matches that returned by `recommend`. All tests pass, though
one is empty and others report a warning because I'm not 100% certain I understand what the
corresponding `nextBest` call is doing.

I've created custom `knit_print` methods for both new classes, and a `tidy` method for
`RecommendationProbs` (`Recommendation` can use the default `tidy` method).

### Sample usage

The simplest `NextBest` rules simply return a suggested dose. `NextBestMTD` is one such class.

```{r}
mtd_next_best <- NextBestMTD(
  target = 0.33,
  derive = function(mtd_samples) {
    quantile(mtd_samples, probs = 0.25)
  }
)

recommend_mtd <- recommend(
  nextBest = mtd_next_best,
  doselimit = next_max_dose,
  samples = my_samples,
  model = my_model,
  data = my_data
)

recommend_mtd
```

Here's the raw return object...

```{r}
normal_print(recommend_mtd)
```

and the prettified version, with and without units.

```{r}
recommend_mtd
knit_print(recommend_mtd, unit = "mg/dL")
```

Here's the result of tidying the object.

```{r}
recommend_mtd %>% tidy()
```

The next simplest classes return matrices of probabilities. As discussed above, this is now a
`tibble` in the new methods.

```{r}
# Define the rule which will be used to select the next best dose
# based on the 'NextBestEWOC' class.
ewoc_next_best <- NextBestEWOC(
  target = 0.30,
  overdose = c(0.35, 1),
  max_overdose_prob = 0.25
)

# Calculate the next best dose.
dose_recommendation <- recommend(
  nextBest = ewoc_next_best,
  doselimit = next_max_dose,
  samples = my_samples,
  model = my_model,
  data = my_data
)

```

```{r}
normal_print(dose_recommendation)
knit_print(dose_recommendation, unit = "mg/dL")
```

And for `NextBestNCRM`...

```{r}
nrcm_next_best <- NextBestNCRM(
  target = c(0.2, 0.35),
  overdose = c(0.35, 1),
  max_overdose_prob = 0.25
)

# Calculate the next best dose.
dose_recommendation <- nextBest(
  nextBest = nrcm_next_best,
  doselimit = next_max_dose,
  samples = my_samples,
  model = my_model,
  data = my_data
)
dose_recommendation <- nextBest(
  nextBest = nrcm_next_best,
  doselimit = next_max_dose,
  samples = my_samples,
  model = my_model,
  data = my_data
)

dr <- recommend(
  nextBest = nrcm_next_best,
  doselimit = next_max_dose,
  samples = my_samples,
  model = my_model,
  data = my_data
)

knit_print(dr)
normal_print(dr)
```

> then we could, for convenience, add `Eligible` and/or `Safe` columns to the tibble...

> We could also add slots to the `RecommendationProbs` class to allow for customisation of the
> probabilities table without resort to the `knit_print` method. Obvious choices are `caption` and
> `col.names`.

## Plots

The `plot` methods assume the new `Recommendation` object is passed in the `x` parameter to the
method. The `NextBest` object is passed in the `y` parameter, to permit different behaviours for
`NextBest` classes that share a common `Recommendation` return value.

Here's the simplest example, for a combination of `Recommendation` and `NextBestMTD`.

```{r}
#| echo: FALSE

my_data <- Data(
  x = c(0.1, 0.5, 1.5, 3, 6, 10, 10, 10),
  y = c(0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 0),
  ID = 1:8,
  cohort = c(0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 5, 5),
  doseGrid = c(0.1, 0.5, 1.5, 3, 6, seq(from = 10, to = 80, by = 10))
)

my_model <- LogisticLogNormal(
  mean = c(-0.85, 1),
  cov = matrix(c(1, -0.5, -0.5, 1), nrow = 2),
  ref_dose = 56
)

my_options <- McmcOptions(burnin = 5, step = 1, samples = 1000)
my_samples <- mcmc(my_data, my_model, my_options)

my_increments <- IncrementsRelative(
  intervals = c(0, 20),
  increments = c(1, 0.33)
)
next_max_dose <- maxDose(my_increments, data = my_data)

mtd_next_best <- NextBestMTD(
  target = 0.33,
  derive = function(mtd_samples) {
    quantile(mtd_samples, probs = 0.25)
  }
)
```

```{r}
dr <- recommend(
  nextBest = mtd_next_best,
  doselimit = next_max_dose,
  samples = my_samples,
  model = my_model,
  data = my_data
)

plot(
  dr, 
  mtd_next_best, 
  doselimit = next_max_dose, 
  samples = my_samples,
  model = my_model, 
  data = my_data
)
```

Compared to

```{r}
dr1 <- nextBest(
  nextBest = mtd_next_best,
  doselimit = next_max_dose,
  samples = my_samples,
  model = my_model,
  data = my_data
)

dr1$plot
```

> There is much duplication of arguments passed to different methods as the analysis proceeds. There
> may be some mileage in creating slots in `Recommendation` to store the inputs on which it was
> based. (For example, `Recommendation` could have a slot for the `NextBest` rule on which it was
> based. This would remove the need to pass both objects to subsequent `plot` calls. And potentially
> reduce the risk of error.) This would allow simplification of future calls, but would be a
> departure from current practice.
